title: The Two Sides of the Stress Coin: Dissociable Cortisol and Noradrenergic Effects on Neural Circuits for Parochial Cooperation and Competition – A Pharmacological fMRI Study
summary: Stress can influence how people behave toward members of their own group (that is, a group they feel affiliated with) and toward other groups. However, it is not yet fully understood why stress may sometimes promote cooperation and at other times increase competition. This study investigates how different components of the body's stress response affect social decision-making and brain activity. Healthy adults are randomly assigned to one of three groups and receive either one of two study medications that change distinct components of the physiological stress response, or a placebo. They then complete a decision-making task while their brain activity is measured using magnetic resonance imaging. In addition, saliva samples, heart rate and blood pressure measurements, and questionnaires are collected. The aim is to better understand how stress-related biological processes influence cooperation, competition, and the brain mechanisms involved in these decisions.
conditions: Stress-related biological processes and social decision-making in healthy adults

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Healthy adults aged 18–50 years; written informed consent; MRI eligibility; sufficient proficiency in German to understand the study information and instructions; right-handedness; BMI between 19 and 26 kg/m²; willingness to comply with study-specific restrictions regarding medication, alcohol, caffeine, food intake and physical activity. Female participants of childbearing potential must have a regular menstrual cycle, use no hormonal or intrauterine contraception, use exclusively non-hormonal barrier contraception, and provide a negative on-site pregnancy test prior to study medication administration.
Exclusion criteria:
Pregnancy or breastfeeding, or refusal of pregnancy testing; current or previous relevant medical, neurological or psychiatric disorders; regular use of prescription medication, particularly centrally active substances, beta-blockers, steroids or cortisone-containing preparations; use of over-the-counter analgesics within 48 hours before testing or any medication within 24 hours before testing; cardiovascular disorders, abnormal blood pressure or cardiac arrhythmias; smoking or vaping within the previous 6 months; use of illegal drugs or psychotropic substances; excessive alcohol consumption (>40 g pure alcohol/day on average on at least 4 days/week for at least 6 months); BMI below 19 or above 26 kg/m²; hormonal contraceptive use within the previous 6 months or use of an intrauterine device; MRI contraindications such as non-MRI-compatible metallic implants or medical devices, claustrophobia or epilepsy; left-handedness; acute sleep deprivation, acute illness, or failure to comply with the study-specific pre-testing restrictions.
